Neonates of Darevskia valentini emerge from parchment-shelled eggs after a prolonged incubation period, exhibiting a snout-vent length at hatching of 2.53 centimetres [Lb = 2.53 centimetres]. This modest size at emergence is typical for the genus and reflects the constraints of yolk-dependent embryonic development within the cleidoic egg. Field surveys of newly hatched cohorts from across the species' range in the Lesser Caucasus indicate that the initial body length is remarkably consistent, with little inter-population variation attributable to maternal effects or local thermal regimes. Following eclosion, the lecithotrophic larvae, which in this oviparous species are fully formed hatchlings, rapidly commence exogenous feeding on small arthropods.

As juvenile lizards progress through successive growth seasons, their body dimensions increase steadily, eventually approaching the asymptotic snout-vent length that defines the adult morphology. Comparative studies among Caucasian rock lizards have demonstrated that males and females ultimately converge on a similar maximum body size, with the ultimate snout-vent length recorded at 7.37 centimetres [Li = 7.37 centimetres] in the largest adults from the Armenian highlands. However, this upper bound is not uniform across all populations; an alternative assessment conducted on a large sample from the Trialeti range reported a mean asymptotic SVL of 6.39 centimetres [Li = 6.39 centimetres], suggesting that local ecological conditions, such as resource availability and intraspecific competition, can modulate the growth plateau.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], which mimics the optimal active-season thermal environment for this montane species, several key life-history parameters have been quantified. At this temperature, females lay up to approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year], each containing around 5 eggs [N_R_i = each containing around 5 eggs], corresponding to a maximum reproductive output of about 10 eggs per year under ideal feeding conditions. This estimate represents the upper boundary of what is physiologically achievable for Darevskia valentini, though natural populations rarely sustain such output, given seasonal constraints and the energetic demands of yolk production and egg retention.

The same thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] also provided the context for estimating longevity in this species. Although wild individuals face substantial mortality from predation and harsh alpine winters, captive-reared Caucasian rock lizards have exhibited a maximum lifespan of approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This extended lifespan, which is considerable for a lizard of its body size, likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality encountered in a controlled environment, combined with a relatively slow pace of ageing. In contrast, field-based mark-recapture studies suggest that most adults in natural populations survive for only three to five active seasons, with senescence apparent in the form of reduced locomotor performance and tail regeneration capacity among older individuals.

Reproductive maturation in Darevskia valentini occurs well before the attainment of ultimate body size. Under constant conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], females reach the age at first reproduction at 2 years after hatching [tR = 2 years after hatching]. This delay reflects the prolonged period required for gonadal activation and the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support vitellogenesis and egg production. The maximum adult wet body mass attained by reproductively mature females is 11.83 grams [Wwi = 11.83 grams], which represents the asymptotic mass under ad libitum feeding regimes. This combination of a moderately late first breeding event and a modest adult mass underscores a life-history strategy oriented toward stable, iteroparous reproduction rather than rapid, early resource allocation to offspring.
